Accuracy check (2026-10-21). The You Are the Reason Tour began July 22, 2026 (Mexico City) and is in its North American arena leg in October 2026; the hometown finale is two nights at Madison Square Garden, November 23-24, 2026, with Oceania and European legs through July 14, 2027 (S37, S08, S16). 2026 singles: "Homewrecker" (February 6), "Potential" (April 17), "My Body Isn’t Ready" (June 25). The second album is in progress (ELLE, September 22, 2026) but its title and date are unannounced; fan wikis list a possible working title, not confirmed. He opened the George Michael tribute at the September 27, 2026 VMAs, drew online criticism and had made no public response as of today. He received Variety’s songwriter honor from Lindsey Buckingham on August 5, 2026, and was among the most-awarded artists (three wins) at the May 25, 2026 AMAs. The backlog note’s "possible Grammy noms Nov 16" was not verified and should not be printed. open_case.next_review is 2026-12-15, after the Garden shows and any year-end album or awards news.

Drafting guidance (open case). Follow the standard’s "Open case profiles" section. Open with who he is and why people are searching (the arena tour ending at Madison Square Garden; Swift’s "Sombr is the future"), then name the open question: is "somber" the self or the image? The strongest verified, durable hook: in November 2023, at 18 and with no hit, he told 1883 Magazine that Madison Square Garden was his dream, "but it will happen. I know it!" (S17). In November 2026 he headlines it twice, and in June 2026 he told Jimmy Fallon his life goal had been "a 1,000-seater" (S16). Other strong verified details: Variety’s tally of "cocky" 12 times and "grateful" 12 times (C20); his line, in his childhood bedroom, that he never felt good at anything "until other people told me that I was good" (C14); A/B testing choruses on TikTok (C13); fighting Tony Berg to keep imperfect vocals (C18); the ELLE writer watching him watch her listen (C32). Show the record dated and sourced, with its limits. Set Three beside Four and Seven with the best evidence for and against each, and say plainly what professional incentive explains (TikTok strategy, image care, authenticity talk as an answer to industry-plant claims). Include an H2 beginning "## What would settle it" built from open_case.settle_signals. Keep "## What is Sombr’s personality type?" with an answer of at most 60 words in "leading read, held loosely" language, e.g. "Leading read: Type 3, held loosely. Type 4 is the live alternative, with 7 still in play." Target 1,200-2,500 words. Titles, description and FAQs must say "leading read" or "open case", never "is a Type 3". Set enneagram: 3, type: ['celebrity'] per site convention, published: false. Use his stage name as he styles it in running text per site convention (the press uses both "Sombr" and "sombr"); his legal name is Shane Michael Boose.

Quotation cautions. (a) S09-S16, S33 and S38 are YouTube caption transcripts without reliable speaker labels; check every printed quote against the audio at the timestamp in the source locator, keep or mark disfluencies honestly, and do not tidy the wording into something he did not say. S16 (Fallon) captions look professionally made but still need checking. (b) The NPR transcript (S05) is provisional by NPR’s own note. (c) Variety and i-D both misname the album "I Barely Knew Her"; the title is I Barely Know Her. (d) American Songwriter wrongly says he won "best alternative artist" at the VMAs; it was Best Alternative Video for "Back to Friends". (e) Swift’s New York Times quote is via L’Officiel (S27); open the NYT interview before quoting it as the Times. Her October 2025 SiriusXM remark was not opened; describe it only generally. (f) His George Michael quotes are from Vogue via Billboard (S28); attribute as "told Vogue". (g) "The biggest artist in the world" is a phrase inside People’s paraphrase (S20); attribute it as reported. (h) The "bark"/"daddy" allegations are the TikTok critic’s claims as relayed by Complex and the Daily Collegian (S24, S25), not observed. (i) Cover Media, Rova, ARY News, The Tab, Tribune and BollywoodShaadis only syndicate the Variety and ELLE quotes; cite the originals (S07, S08). (j) Variety’s "cocky" and "grateful" counts are the writer’s tallies, not a transcript. (k) Do not attribute the Lindsey Buckingham quote to Sombr: Buckingham is speaking (S32). (l) ELLE’s "inked his record deal with Warner Records at 16" conflicts with the January 2023 announcement at 17 (S18); use "at 17" for the signing.

Sensitivity. Mental health: he has disclosed depression (lifelong, and a "deep, deep depression" in 2026 with "darker points than I’ve ever seen" and not being able to "see a future"), anxiety attacks, eating difficulties and body-image distress (C22, C33-C35). Use these only in his words, dated and in context, without diagnostic labels ("eating disorder", "clinical") and without speculation about risk; never use them as type evidence; never make them the hook or the ending; and do not quote the "can’t see a future" line in isolation or in a headline, description or FAQ. Do not quote the People line about dying and being remembered (S20) or the Virginia Woolf reference in 1883 (S17). If the draft discusses his 2026 depression disclosure at any length, follow responsible-reporting practice (no sensational framing; consider a brief support-resource note consistent with site practice). Allegations: attribute every concert-behavior claim to the TikTok critic, give his responses then and in 2026 (C26, C27), and do not repeat "bark"/"daddy" as fact. Present the industry-plant charge as an allegation with his rebuttal and the documented facts (his father’s company; his father on his team), and do not adjudicate (C28). Privacy: do not name or characterize his sister; do not identify the people behind "Back to Friends" or "Homewrecker"; do not repeat dating rumors (an Addison Rae dinner was tabloid fodder); mention teenage cannabis use only in his words, if at all. Do not characterize his private relationship with Taylor Swift.

sources.title: Can Sombr Save Rock ‘n’ Roll? (Sombr Interview on His Debut Album, Addison Rae, and Rock Stardom)
sources.speaker: Sombr (Shane Boose), interviewed in person at the Chateau Marmont and by phone by Douglas Greenwood (i-D)
sources.date: 2025-08-18 (byline date on the saved page; Wikipedia cites August 17, 2025)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2-4 (album unfinished days before deadline; "Is my mind going insane"; "They don’t come out of a fucking factory"); paragraph 5 (writes alone at night, Tony Berg "my mentor", "No co-writers or committees"); paragraph 6 (ex texted after Fallon; "if all art was hiding the truth"); paragraph 7 (online persona; "I actually can’t read"); paragraph 8 (Lower East Side childhood, "very emotionally complicated child", father present and nodding); paragraphs 11-12 ("I will never think it’s complete"); closing phone call ("I would pay to be on tour", "closest thing to drugs", "I’m so grateful that people know who I am"); paragraph 9 ('his dad had a stint in a band'); paragraph 6 ('He’s recounting the messages to me, and then shrugging them off')
sources.excerpt: “Is my mind going insane, or are people gonna like this?” [...] “They don’t come out of a fucking factory.” [...] “That’s my mentor,” he says. “Fucking best guy ever.” That’s it. No co-writers or committees. [...] “It’s definitely got me in trouble, but if all art was hiding the truth, art would fucking suck,” [...] “I was a very emotionally complicated child,” he says. “My dad can confirm that.” [...] “But you can’t make music without being a little bit crazy.” [...] “There’s not necessarily something missing, it’s just that I will never think it’s complete,” [...] “I would pay to be on tour,” [...] “the closest thing to drugs.” [...] “I’m so grateful that people know who I am,” he says. “It’s just the life I chose. [...] Recently, after performing “Back to Friends” on Fallon, he came off stage to several texts and missed calls from the girl it’s about. [...] He’s recounting the messages to me, and then shrugging them off. [...] his dad had a stint in a band (they weren’t big, so it doesn’t count as a nepo thing)
sources.context: Long reported cover profile from early August 2025, before the album release and before the Grammy nomination, with his father sitting beside him (the writer reports the father nodding at "very emotionally complicated child"). Observations (the "hot waif", the self-satirizing TikTok persona) are the writer’s. The writer misnames the album "I Barely Knew Her" in two places; do not copy that. The ex who texted after Fallon is not named; keep her unnamed. Draft stage: the saved page text carries the byline date AUGUST 18, 2025.

sources.title: Sombr ‘Didn’t Want to Just Do Ballads Forever’ — So He Pushed the Tempo and Scored Two Hot 100 Hits
sources.speaker: Sombr (Shane Boose), interviewed by Jason Lipshutz (Billboard)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 1-2 (Radiohead, Buckley, Bridgers); paragraph on streaming totals ("They 100 percent break my brain"); paragraph on "Caroline" and the signing; paragraph beginning "Sombr, who still writes and produces all of his songs" ("I’m a really hard worker... manifest"); "I didn’t want to just do ballads forever"; closing ("It’s all I’ve ever wanted").
sources.excerpt: “They 100 percent break my brain,” he says of the streaming totals. [...] “I was just making music,” he says, “and I’m a really hard worker. I like to think that, if you really put in the hours and manifest what you want, it will happen.” [...] “I didn’t want to just do ballads forever.” [...] “It’s getting wild, and I love it. It’s all I’ve ever wanted.”
sources.context: Trade-press interview during his breakout, when "Back to Friends" was climbing the Hot 100 and he was opening for Daniel Seavey. Note that the claim he "never got impatient" while waiting for a breakthrough conflicts with his later accounts of discouragement and fear of being dropped (S04, S09).

sources.title: For Artists Like Gigi Perez and Sombr, Self-Producing Is ‘An Experiment and an Adventure’
sources.speaker: Sombr, interviewed by Jason Lipshutz (Billboard); feature also covers Gigi Perez
sources.locator: Sombr paragraphs: "It’s authentic, straight from me"; GarageBand at the end of elementary school, Logic in middle school, never considered another producer; "hit-making factory"; 50-70% at home then Sound City with Tony Berg; "I am old-fashioned... I agonize over lyrics."
sources.excerpt: “It’s authentic, straight from me,” [...] he says he never considered relying upon another producer for his work. [...] “It’s just me in my room, making stuff that I want to hear and based off what I feel. And that’s why it works in my mind.” [...] “I agonize over lyrics. I really have no interest in AI and how it relates to music.”
sources.context: Trade feature on self-producing pop artists, a week before his album release. The "factory" and "straight from me" framing recurs across 2025 and doubles as his answer to industry-plant talk (C28).

sources.title: December 2025 Digital Cover Story: The Unfiltered Rise of Sombr, Whose Vulnerability, and DIY Vision Launched a New Kind of Pop Star
sources.speaker: Sombr, interviewed at his Los Angeles home by Lily Moayeri (American Songwriter)
sources.locator: Paragraph 3 ("I couldn’t imagine my 17-year-old self"); paragraph on Berg’s reading list ("It felt like homework"); paragraph on the post-signing slump ("I was definitely discouraged... you get dropped"); paragraph on "back to friends" ("Everything before ‘back to friends’..."); Sound City paragraph ("I want to impress Tony"); distortion paragraph; depression paragraph ("My whole life I’ve dealt with some aspect of that"); closing paragraphs ("my world has lost its innocence", "the world needs more individuals").; process paragraph ('Before he brings a song to Berg'); 'Interestingly, back to friends was made without Berg's production involvement'; LaGuardia/'caroline' paragraph ('went viral on TikTok overnight', 'signed to Warner Records in quick order'); slump paragraph ('My ego was stroked so hard'; 'nearly three years... almost 20 songs')
sources.excerpt: “I was definitely discouraged,” he says. “I was signed at 17. My ego was stroked so hard. I left school. I was making a bunch of stuff and wasn’t seeing the numbers my label had hoped for, which was really hard because I was so passionate about the music. When all of a sudden you’re thrown into a commercial thing, and you’re competing, if you don’t do numbers within a certain amount of time, you get dropped. That was a big fear I definitely felt creeping in.” [...] “Everything before ‘back to friends’ was me making what I thought people wanted to hear, or what I thought would work,” says sombr. “That just wasn’t the truth. It’s a mind fuck having your passion become a job. ‘back to friends’ was when I got past that and said, ‘I’m going to make what I feel like making.’” [...] “Now, every time I write a song at home, I want to impress Tony. I don’t want him to have notes. I don’t want to bring anything other than a song better than the song I brought the last time. He really pushed me in that way. I have high standards for myself. [...] “My whole life I’ve dealt with some aspect of that, and I was trying to figure it out, still figuring it out,” [...] “To be honest, my world has lost its innocence,” he says. “Everything is a much more real now and feels like work. I want to make a project without anything in mind. I want to do more of what I want.” [...] “But I think the world needs more individuals in music.” [...] Before he brings a song to Berg, sombr completes it at home, alone, the only way he can be truly vulnerable. [...] Interestingly, “back to friends” was made without Berg’s production involvement. [...] in the nearly three years between “caroline” and “back to friends,” sombr released almost 20 songs, none of which made a significant impact. [...] He dropped out of LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts [...] during his junior year after his self-written and recorded song “caroline,” [...] went viral on TikTok overnight. He was signed to Warner Records in quick order, moved to Los Angeles, and found a creative mentor in esteemed producer Tony Berg [...] “When I first started going to Sound City, I thought I was the shit, but I was not,” [...] “I was signed at 17. My ego was stroked so hard. I left school.”
sources.context: The most reflective print interview of the 2025 cycle, given just after the Grammy nomination. "That" in "My whole life I’ve dealt with some aspect of that" refers to being depressed, which the writer paraphrases immediately before the quote; quote it with that context. The piece wrongly says he won "best alternative artist" at the VMAs; the award was Best Alternative Video (S34).

sources.title: The artist known as sombr discusses his new album, growing up in New York and more (NPR Weekend Edition Sunday)

sources.locator: NPR transcript: opening ("it really, really does feel like suffering"); Lower East Side answer; LaGuardia arias answer; distortion answer; closing exchange on love ("I don’t think I’ve been truly in love", "I felt so obsessed").
sources.excerpt: BOOSE: I definitely have experienced many times seeing, you know, the one I loved with someone else, and it's really - the feeling you get when you see that and you still haven't moved on is like - it really, really does feel like suffering. [...] I like the amount of distortion on the vocal to reflect how emotional what I'm singing is about. [...] No, I don't think I've figured it out because I don't - I don't think I've been truly in love. [...] I felt so obsessed and like I would be with this person for the rest of my life, and I would do anything for this person.
sources.context: Short public-radio interview two weeks after the album release. NPR notes its transcripts are produced on deadline and may differ from the audio; check printed quotes against the broadcast.

[...] it has forced him to “always look camera-ready.” [...] He was more concerned about what his peers would say in group chats than about making it big. [...] “When you’re in high school, you’re scared to be judged.” [...] “But then I realized, ‘Wait, you guys also want to own my music. So I deserve a lot more than dinner.’” [...] “Either I’ll be a high school dropout and also be dropped by my label, or I’ll be a high school-dropout success story.” [...] Boose, who describes himself as cocky (the word comes up 12 times in our interview), credits Berg with keeping him “in check” and teaching him to have higher standards for his writing. “I thought I knew everything,” Boose says, “and he basically showed me that I knew nothing, and that I had a lot of work to do.” [...] “I’m a kid who dropped out of high school who now has a crew of 30 people on tour with me,” he says, “and they’re looking to me to lead the charge.” [...] “Touring is the biggest high you can get as an artist,” he says. “For me, it’s more about how I can survive not being on tour.” [...] “I’m OK with people knowing everything about me,” [...] “Now, I’ve just accepted it. Everyone can say whatever the fuck they want about me. I know who I am.” [...] “I want people who look up to me that might not be happy about their body image to understand that I’m not always happy about my body image,” [...] “I asked Taylor to pick the songs for me, because I wanted the night to be fully about her, but she wouldn’t allow it,” he says. “She was like, ‘No, I want you to pick the songs.’ It put me under a lot of pressure, but she was really happy with my choices.” [...] “I have issues with eating,” he says. [...] “Most of the time before shows I’m literally eating against my will, so I have enough energy to get through the show.” [...] “It’s been my lifelong struggle. I only eat to survive; I don’t eat for pleasure most of the time.” [...] “Does she just like me for the things I do?” he sings suspiciously of a love interest on “My Body Isn’t Ready.” (“That’s a lyric I couldn’t have written a year ago,” Boose notes.) [...] “I don’t want to date someone who wants to date me for the wrong reasons.” [...] Validating his adolescent ego trip was an email from Columbia Records sitting in his inbox when he got home from school. Boose’s dad warned him not to reply. “That’s a scam,” he said. [...] “But it wasn’t a scam,” Boose says [...] The emails from record companies continued to roll in, with Warner Records flying the 16-year-old to Los Angeles for a meeting. [...] his label hooked him up with veteran producer Tony Berg, who helped launch Phoebe Bridgers’ career.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The somber self-description is consistent across 2023-2026 and settings: the name 'kind of made sense for how I was feeling' (C02), 'a very emotionally complicated child' (C15), 'teenage angst and rejection' (C15b), writing alone because it is 'vulnerable' and because 'I love being in my own head' (C16, C16e), and 'I just feel out of place in the regular world and in public' (C23b). Identification with feeling fits Four more naturally than Three. (2) His own account of the breakthrough is a turn away from 'what I thought would work' toward 'what I feel like making' (C06, C06b), and he keeps authorship habits: imperfection kept against his mentor (C18), solo writing (C16, C16b), confessional lyrics that got him 'in trouble' (C37, C37b), and a stated wish to 'go back to my roots... that is truly me' (C38, C38d). These costs are small, and confession is also the commercial formula (C37c). (3) Much of the Three material is the job: TikTok-era careers require testing hooks, posting daily and studying the algorithm (C12, C12b, C12c, C13). He says he tests because he likes to (C13c), which weakens but does not remove the discount. (4) The fears that carried the Three case (being dropped, being 'a disappointment', C05, C05b) fit a Six's fear of losing support as readily, and the core CBS answer is as much about belonging as about ability (C14, C14g, C14k, C14d); the tape may also contain him saying 'I don't believe them' about praise (C14h), which would cut against worth settled by others' verdict. (5) The modest Fallon line is talk-show register; the NYLON and Broski 'odds' lines are not a retreat from ambition (C11b, C11e, C11g). (6) His October 2025 to 2026 change of stance includes a concession on substance and a commitment about conduct, not only reception management (C27b, C27d, C27c, I14). (7) Almost everything is self-report in promotional settings since spring 2025; third-party testimony comes from friends, collaborators and admirers (C31, C32), and no one who knew him before 2022 is on record (I12). Mental-health and body-image disclosures are excluded from the argument entirely (C35, I16).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4 explains the emotional center of the record and leads on how he describes his inner life. He named himself for a mood (C02; 'teenage angst and rejection', C15b), was 'a very emotionally complicated child' (C15), never felt he belonged (C14g, C14k), and says he is most himself on stage and feels 'out of place in the regular world and in public' (C23b). He writes alone because it is vulnerable and because he loves 'being in my own head' (C16, C16e), keeps imperfection against expert advice (C18), confesses at some cost (C37, C37b), narrates his breakthrough as abandoning what would work (C06, C06b), and after the pop hits said the indie self 'is truly me' (C38, C38d). What strains Four: his method hands unfinished songs to the crowd and finishes what it likes, and he says he enjoys that (C13, C13b, C13c, I08); he resists being set apart ('a little too normal', C41, discounted as promo register); he works to leave his mentor with no notes (C19); and he holds onto status ('I will always be a Grammy nominee', C44). Envy is not observed, but promotional interviews rarely surface it. Type 6 is live: the named fears (dropped, 'a disappointment') are fears of losing support (I20); belonging recurs in the CBS answer (C14g, C14k); he avoids going out after shows so he will not 'let down my fans' (C48, C48b); he read label courtship as 'you guys also want to own my music' (C49); and he credits Berg with keeping him 'in check' (S07). Against Six: his bets are unhedged (leaving school at 17 with his father's backing, moving to Los Angeles at 18, posting a song daily until it hit; C04, C07b), though a counterphobic Six also charges at fear (I20b). Type 7 is live: touring is 'the biggest high' and the problem is surviving 'not being on tour' (C23c), he slept through his nominations because he 'can't deal with the pressure of like waiting for the moment' (C42), his online persona is unserious (C27), and Quenlin Blackwell describes him as 'so happy, ready, and willing to explore and create' (C31). Against Seven: his named fears concern judgment, failure and letting people down, and the songs stay with pain rather than reframing it (I09b). Type 2 was considered and set aside: 'a people pleaser' is a comic bit and nothing shows a helper identity (C45, I10).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: None that is defensible yet. The best candidate separates Three from Four: when what feels true and what works pull apart at a cost, which wins (I01b, I21)? The record points both ways. For Three, the motives that survive the professional-incentive discount are few and self-reported: he says he tests songs because he likes to, not because he must (C13c); the judge he writes for is one person whose notes he wants to avoid (C19); his authenticity turn came only after 'it wasn't working anymore' (C06f, I17); and he treats a Grammy nomination as permanent status (C44). For Four, his self-description is consistent and his authorship habits persist (C02, C15, C16e, C23b, C18, C38). Three therefore leads on a tiebreaker (I07, I07b), not a margin. Six is not separated from Three by the named fears, which fit both (I20); what would separate them is whether, under pressure, he seeks security and trusted support or recognition. Seven cannot be excluded until he is seen through a long stretch off tour (C23c, C53). The decisive tests are the second album and his account of it, a first commercial setback, his next reason for writing alone, his next sustained public criticism, and the first long break from touring (open_case.settle_signals). None had happened as of October 21, 2026, so Three cannot be held above low confidence and the profile is an open case.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why a musician who, by his account, began studying the social media algorithm in his early teens (C12, C12d) named himself for a mood at about the same age (S18 says he adopted the moniker at 14) and says he is most himself on stage while feeling out of place elsewhere (C23b). Why he says he never knew he was good until others told him, despite years of musical theater and a classical vocal major's training at LaGuardia (C14b, C14i).
